title: Friday: al-Kahf
tomorrow: there's an hour on Friday nobody can pin down. when is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: ready for friday, washed and scented before the call. The prayer ends at midday, but the day is still Friday, and one surah belongs to it.
screen: `READY FOR FRIDAY.` → `THE REST OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Somebody asks how long you've lived in your town, and you round it: about three years. Surah al-Kahf, the Cave, the surah a report gives its own Friday light, has a stranger number in it. Young men flee into a cave and fall asleep. For how long? The text gives it as three hundred years, and then it adds nine. Not three hundred and nine. Three hundred, add nine. And the very next verse says God knows best how long they stayed. Why give a number, then hand the counting back?
screen: `ABOUT THREE YEARS.` → `THE CAVE, AND ITS FRIDAY LIGHT.` → `300, ADD NINE.` → `WHY HAND THE COUNT BACK?`

segments.voice: First, the Friday part. A report from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, collected by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, says whoever reads al-Kahf on Friday has a light that shines for them between the two Fridays. Hadith scholars grade that report differently, so it's held with care. Now the puzzle. Some commentators read the odd wording as two calendars: three hundred years by the sun, three hundred and nine by the moon. Others read the verse as reporting what people said, then correcting them: God knows best. Either way, the number isn't the point. Look at what the whole surah keeps doing with time. The sleepers wake up and guess they stayed a day, or part of a day. A man walks through his garden and says he doesn't think it will ever perish; by the end of his story, it's ruined. Musa follows a teacher, al-Khidr, and can't wait to understand; three times he asks too soon. And tucked in the middle, a small instruction: never say of anything, I'll do that tomorrow, without adding, if God wills. People misjudging time, again and again. Read that every Friday and the week gets measured against something bigger than the week. That's one way to hear the friday light: a long reading that resets how you count.
screen: `A LIGHT BETWEEN TWO FRIDAYS.` · `300 BY THE SUN, 309 BY THE MOON?` · `A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY.` · `IF GOD WILLS.` · then, large: `THE FRIDAY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Open al-Kahf in any translation you have, and read its opening verses out loud, slowly, for the length of the sit. If you know the Arabic, read that instead. A few verses is a real start; next Friday, pick up where you stopped.
Friday, and its surah: al-Kahf, the Cave, read from one Friday to the next, with a light the report says lasts between them.
Hold on to this: the friday light is a long reading that measures the week against more than the week. Two days into the weekly rhythm.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep this practice read Surah al-Kahf (surah 18) on Fridays, alone or with family; some read it in one sitting, others a little at a time through the day.

fork.setup: your friend says she'll definitely finish her essay tomorrow, no question, it's handled. which line from al-Kahf fits?
options: 'if God wills': make the plan, and hold tomorrow loosely.
'three hundred, add nine': deadlines are flexible anyway.
'a day or part of a day': she has more time than she thinks.
fork.reveal: al-Kahf says never say I'll do that tomorrow without adding if God wills. it isn't against plans; it's against being sure of tomorrow.

al-Kahf.meaning: the Cave: surah 18 of the Qur'an

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.meaning: a companion who passed on the Friday-light report

al-Khidr.meaning: the teacher Musa follows in surah 18

Musa.meaning: Moses, a prophet in the Qur'an

sources.ref: al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra (Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: whoever reads al-Kahf on Friday, a light shines for him between the two Fridays)
Qur'an 18:19 (a day or part of a day); 18:25–26 (three hundred years, and add nine; God knows best how long they stayed)
Qur'an 18:32–42 (the man of the two gardens); 18:60–82 (Musa and his teacher; three questions); 18:23–24 (if God wills)
Ibn Kathir, Tafsir on 18:25 (the solar and lunar reading of 'add nine')

notes: The Friday-light report is graded differently (some hold it marfu', some mawquf on Abu Sa'id); the script says only that it's 'held with care'. Confirm the references in al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi.
The solar/lunar reading of 18:25 attributed to 'some commentators' (Ibn Kathir among them); the alternative reading (reporting what people said) also attributed generally. Confirm both.
Qur'an passages paraphrased throughout (no quotation marks): 18:19, 18:23–26, 18:35, 18:60–82. 'Three times he asks too soon' refers to 18:71, 18:74, 18:77.
Naming al-Khidr: the Qur'an says 'one of Our servants'; the name comes from the hadith (Bukhari 122). Fine to keep, but a Keeper may want that said.
